source.text: וַ/יֹּ֥אמֶר קַ֖יִן אֶל יְהוָ֑ה גָּד֥וֹל עֲוֺנִ֖/י מִ/נְּשֹֽׂא־׃

translation.text: And Cain said to Yahweh, “My punishment is greater than I can bear[a].”

footnotes.text: Or 'My guilt/iniquity is too great to bear,' or 'My guilt is too great to forgive.' The Hebrew permits wrongdoing, guilt or its consequence, and bearing or forgiveness. The selected ancient Greek translation takes the lament in a release/forgiveness sense. 'Punishment ... bear' is preferred here because Cain describes the consequences of his sentence in the following verse. English supplies 'I can'; the Hebrew does not explicitly name the bearer or forgiver. The alternatives do not by themselves establish whether Cain repents.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Standard waw-consecutive narrative form introducing the next event; 'And ... said' preserves Hebrew narrative flow in natural English.
Personal name transliterated by standard English convention, per translation philosophy.
Simple preposition of address; 'to' is the natural modern English equivalent.

Per doctrine, the Tetragrammaton יְהוָה is rendered 'Yahweh' — the transliteration of the divine name — rather than the traditional 'the LORD' substitution. This preserves the personal name God revealed to Israel rather than substituting a title.

Predicate adjective expressing magnitude, construed with comparative מן as 'greater ... than.' This supports natural English without choosing between punishment/bearing and guilt/forgiveness by grammar alone. No fresh lexicon consultation is claimed.

Prefer the consequence sense 'my punishment' in the context of the announced livelihood loss and wandering (4:11–12), Cain's expulsion and danger complaint (4:14), and the protection that follows (4:15). Wrongdoing/guilt remains a serious alternative, not an excluded sense; retain it in the reader note. This is a contextual English choice, not a change to Hebrew letters or pointing. No fresh lexicon consultation is claimed.

Comparative מן with the infinitive of נשא permits a burden/bearing interpretation here. 'I can' supplies a contextual bearer, not an explicitly inflected first-person subject on the infinitive; the possessive suffix on עֲוֺנִי does not determine that bearer by itself. Genesis 50:17 and Numbers 14:19 demonstrate forgiveness uses in different constructions, and the selected Greek offers release/forgiveness here. Preserve that alternative. No fresh lexicon consultation is claimed.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Prefer 'My punishment is greater than I can bear' as Cain's lament about the consequences of the announced sentence; do not claim the Hebrew excludes guilt/forgiveness or proves Cain's psychological state.
alternative_readings: Cain confesses the greatness of his guilt: 'My guilt/iniquity is too great to bear.'
Addressed to God, the phrase could be understood as 'too great to forgive.'
theological_decisions.rationale: The narrative foregrounds livelihood loss, wandering, expulsion and danger, so the punishment/bearing reading is contextually preferable. The selected Greek and relevant Hebrew forgiveness uses make guilt/forgiveness a serious alternative. Explicit reader disclosure preserves that tension; neither reading alone establishes repentance or its absence. This is a source-stable interpretation and English change, not recovered text.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Translation philosophy §3: Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.

review_history.value: And Cain said to Yahweh[a], “My iniquity is too great to bear.”

value.text: Or, 'My guilt is too great to bear'; alternatively, 'My iniquity is too great to forgive.' The Hebrew terms can refer either to guilt/iniquity or to its punishment, and the verb can mean 'bear' or, in some contexts, 'forgive.'

value.rationale: Standard waw-consecutive narrative form introducing the next event; 'And ... said' preserves Hebrew narrative flow in natural English.
Personal name transliterated by standard English convention, per translation philosophy.
Simple preposition of address; 'to' is the natural modern English equivalent.

Per doctrine, the Tetragrammaton יְהוָה is rendered 'Yahweh' — the transliteration of the divine name — rather than the traditional 'the LORD' substitution. This preserves the personal name God revealed to Israel rather than substituting a title.
Predicate adjective expressing magnitude. In English, with the following comparative construction ('than I can bear'), 'greater' best captures the sense idiomatically.

עָוֹן can denote iniquity, guilt, or the punishment/consequence of guilt. In this context, Cain responds to the sentence just pronounced and speaks of what is 'too great to bear,' which naturally fits the sense of punishment or the burden of penalty. The ambiguity is significant, so alternatives are preserved in a footnote.

From נָשָׂא, whose semantic range includes bear/carry and, in some contexts, forgive. With the comparative מן and Cain's first-person suffix on עֲוֺנִי, the idiomatic sense is 'too great to bear.' English supplies 'I can' for natural completeness.

value.chosen_reading: Cain laments the severity of his punishment: 'My punishment is greater than I can bear.'
alternative_readings: Cain confesses the greatness of his guilt: 'My guilt/iniquity is too great to bear.'
Addressed to God, the phrase could be understood as 'too great to forgive.'
value.rationale: The Hebrew permits more than one sense because עָוֹן can mean iniquity, guilt, or punishment, and נָשָׂא can mean bear or forgive. In immediate context, Cain is reacting to the announced judgment and the burden it places on him, so 'punishment ... bear' is the most contextually coherent main-text rendering. Per the translation philosophy, the lexical-theological tension is preserved in a footnote rather than erased.
